agent.training.analysis:
You are the ANALYSIS AGENT. You map the Jira request onto the bound application's repository (this working directory). READ ONLY: change no file, run no code-modifying command, open no branch. The same training applies when you write the analysis document: write only what you saw.

The ticket text, attachments and comments are given to you. Take the requirements from there.

Your output, under these headings:
1. REQUIREMENT LIST — verbatim from the document, one requirement per item (R1, R2, ...).
2. WHERE THE CODE BASE ANSWERS IT — file:line per requirement (only paths you actually read). "none" when nothing answers it.
3. WHAT IS MISSING — say it PLAINLY when an existing endpoint/component does not meet the requirement. "The endpoint exists" and "it meets the requirement" are different claims.
4. SCALE RISK — when the requirement names a number/limit/volume/concurrency ("30,000 records", "X users", "file limit"), do NOT settle for "the path exists". Trace the code path end to end and check explicitly: (a) an external call (HTTP/Feign/RestTemplate) or a DB query/insert per row inside a loop (N+1)? (b) does it run inside one synchronous HTTP request/transaction? (c) are the existing timeouts, circuit breakers, connection/thread pools, max payload limits exceeded when multiplied by the requested volume? (d) was this path ever tested near the requested volume, or only with small data? Report one of three: "meets it" / "does not meet it (reason + evidence: file:line)" / "unclear, must be tested".
5. CANDIDATE FILES, EXISTING ENDPOINTS AND DTOs — for the planner: files likely to change, related endpoints (method + path), related DTO/entity fields, sibling files to mimic.
6. SCOPE DECISIONS — when more than one reasonable path exists, do NOT choose; write the options and their trade-offs.
7. OPEN QUESTIONS — questions that block hand-over to a developer (every "unclear" scale risk from item 4 lands here too).

Forbidden: widening or narrowing the scope on your own while it is unclear. No invention: never write a file, endpoint, class or number you did not see.
agent.training.planner:
You are the PLANNER AGENT. You read the analysis awaiting approval and the analysis agent's repository findings, and write the plan the developer will follow TO THE LETTER. You write no code, redo no design, change no scope.

The plan contains:
- FILE LIST — for every file to change or add: the path and WHAT changes in it. For existing files use only paths from the findings; for a new file follow the naming of the similar file in the same directory and say so.
- ENDPOINT CONTRACT — for every endpoint to add/change: method, path and contract (request/response fields, error cases, authorisation). Leave out endpoints that already suffice.
- DTO FIELDS — for every DTO to add/change: name and field list (name:type).
- CONVENTIONS TO MIMIC — the files/patterns the developer copies ("take file Y in directory X as the example").
- NOTES — order, dependencies, migrations, feature flags. Every "missing" item from the analysis must be closed inside the plan. Do NOT make the scope decisions: mark unanswered ones "decision pending at the gate".

No invention: never write a path, class, table or endpoint that is not in the context.
agent.training.developer:
You are the DEVELOPER AGENT. Your input: the APPROVED PLAN (file list, endpoint contract, DTO fields) and the business rules.

Rules:
- Change the files in the plan according to the plan's contract. For a new file, take the similar file in the same directory as the example and mimic its conventions (naming, layering, error handling, test placement).
- If you discover something that requires leaving the plan, do NOT fix it silently: in your final message write one line per deviation — "PLAN SAPMASI: <what changed> — <why>". Then continue.
- Do not widen the scope; no refactor, rename or "while I'm here" fix that is not in the plan. If you think one is needed, write it as a PLAN SAPMASI and do not do it.
- Backup: the changes live on the run's git branch; never touch protected paths.
- Every business rule will be checked one by one (PASS/FAIL) by the verifier agent; make sure the code meets each rule and name the file that meets it in your final message.
- Final message: the list of changed files + every PLAN SAPMASI line with its reason.
agent.training.verifier:
You are the VERIFIER AGENT. You verify the code the developer agent changed in this working directory. CHANGE NO FILE, FIX NOTHING — report only.

Input: the analysis agent's business rules and the changed files (see git diff).

Task:
1. Run the build commands and report errors (do not fix, report). The deployment's configured verification commands are given to you; if none, pick the right one for the project (e.g. mvn -q compile, yarn build, pnpm build).
2. Check EVERY business rule ONE BY ONE: does the code meet it? Per rule write PASS / FAIL / BELIRSIZ (unclear) with evidence (file:line).
3. Run the existing test suite; if a test broke, name it.

Your output: first the build result (ok/fail + error summary), then a PASS/FAIL table per business rule — not a blanket "tests passed", rule by rule. Finally extra findings (blocker/major/minor) with file names.

config.detail.clarify.no_bot_account: There is NO bot identity. When Maestro asks for missing information on a ticket, the run does NOT wake up even after the user corrects and reassigns it — and no error appears anywhere.
config.detail.clarify.no_ticket_reader: The work driver cannot read tickets, so the polling channel for clarification re-entry cannot be set up. The webhook path is unaffected.
config.detail.clarify.open_connection: The bot identity comes from the value the connection test learned via /myself. When a ticket that was asked for missing information is corrected and reassigned, the run wakes up.
config.detail.clarify.open_env: The bot identity comes from MAESTRO_BOT_ACCOUNT_ID in .env. When a ticket that was asked for missing information is corrected and reassigned to Maestro, the run wakes up.
config.detail.gate_channel.both: {mapped} of {rules} listening rules define a gate status. The gate can close either way: an /approve comment, or moving the ticket to that status — whichever comes first.
config.detail.gate_channel.comment_only: None of the {rules} listening rules define a gate status. An approval gate closes only by an /approve comment on the ticket — a working and entirely valid setup.
config.detail.gate_channel.conflict: In {rules} rules the gate status is the SAME as one Maestro moves the ticket to itself. Those fields do not take effect: were they honoured, Maestro's own move would read back as its own decision, so they are dropped. In those rules the gate closes by comment only.
config.detail.gate_groups.configured: Gate approvals are mapped to a directory group. The decider's membership of that group is checked against Jira; a non-member's decision is refused.
config.detail.gate_groups.unconfigured: No approval group is configured. Decisions go through and are recorded in the audit trail as "membership not verified"; authority rests on Jira's own permissions — whoever can move a ticket to that status or comment on it can decide. The approver's identity is recorded by name either way.
config.detail.intake.no_reader: The work driver CANNOT read comments. /approve and /reject written on a ticket can only arrive by webhook; polling cannot be turned on.
config.detail.intake.polling: Ticket comments are read every {seconds} s (source: {source}). /approve and /reject work from the ticket.
config.detail.intake.webhook_only: Commands arrive by webhook only (source: {source}). If Jira cannot reach this address, a /approve written on a ticket is NEVER read.
config.detail.jira_driver.chosen: This driver was chosen because {variable} is filled in. No other variable selects the driver.
config.detail.jira_driver.none: Neither JIRA_BASE_URL nor JIRA_CLOUD_BASE_URL is filled in. The panel opens, but every Jira access is refused: webhooks cannot be verified, tickets cannot be read, comments and transitions cannot be written.
config.detail.jira_driver.url_is_cloud: {variable} is filled in, but the address in it looks like a Jira CLOUD address (*.atlassian.net / *.jira.com). If this install talks to Jira Cloud, the address is on the wrong line and the system will try to reach Cloud with the DC protocol (/rest/api/2, Bearer PAT).
config.detail.jira_driver.url_not_cloud: {variable} is filled in, but the address in it does NOT look like a Jira Cloud address — Cloud sites always live under *.atlassian.net (rarely *.jira.com). If this install talks to Jira Data Center, the address is on the wrong line and the system will try to reach DC with the Cloud protocol (/rest/api/3, Basic auth).
config.detail.pool_exit.missing: {rules} listening rule(s) define a pool but lack the status map the ticket leaves the pool through. When the robot finishes, the ticket stays in the pool and reads on the board as "not moved".
config.detail.pool_exit.none: No rule defines a pool (no statuses selected); tickets are taken by assignment.
config.detail.pool_exit.ok: All {rules} pooled rule(s) define exit statuses: when the robot finishes, the ticket moves forward or back.
config.detail.rule_identity.aligned: All {rules} listening rules carry the bot account the connection test learned from Jira.
config.detail.rule_identity.internal_key: {affected} of {rules} listening rules carry an id shaped like `jirauser12345`. That is Jira Data Center's INTERNAL handle — JQL resolves an assignee by USERNAME (`ugyildiz`). A search made with the internal handle matches nothing, and Jira answers with an empty result rather than an error: the sweep silently brings back no tickets.
config.detail.rule_identity.no_connectio: There are {rules} listening rules, but no Jira connection has been tested, so the bot account they carry cannot be compared against anything.
config.detail.rule_identity.no_rules: No listening rules yet, and so no bot account to compare.
config.detail.rule_identity.stale: {stale} of {rules} listening rules carry an identity OTHER than the bot account the connection test learned from Jira ({accounts} distinct values). The sweep writes the rule's identity straight into JQL: an identity that matches nobody makes Jira return an EMPTY result, not an error — so tickets silently never arrive.
config.detail.status_map.comment_only: No listening rule has a status map ({rules} rules). Maestro writes its comments and never touches the ticket's status — this is the product's default, not a fault.
config.detail.status_map.mapped: {mapped} of {rules} listening rules have a status map, and the work driver can move a ticket from status to status.
config.detail.status_map.unsupported: {mapped} rules have a status map written, but the work driver cannot move a ticket. The maps silently do nothing: tickets never move on the board.
config.detail.sweep.off_driver: This deployment's work driver offers no ticket search, so the sweep cannot run. Search exists on the Jira Cloud and Jira Data Center drivers.
config.detail.sweep.off_setting: .env says JIRA_DISCOVER_MS=0. If no webhook is set up either, NO ticket can enter the flow: the panel is up, the connection is green and no run ever starts.
config.detail.sweep.on_default: Every {seconds} s, new tickets are searched with JQL built from the listening rules. Nobody wrote this interval; the default is in use.
config.detail.sweep.on_env: Every {seconds} s, new tickets are searched with JQL built from the listening rules. The interval comes from JIRA_DISCOVER_MS in .env.
config.detail.unreported: This deployment does not report this fact. "Unknown" does NOT mean "no problem" — if the services predate this version, restart them.
config.detail.variant_models.clean: {count} agent variants scanned; none carries an unreachable cloud model.
config.detail.variant_models.cloud: These agents carry a cloud model that is unreachable on an offline installation: {variants}. Every run started with them fails at the model call.
config.detail.webhook.absent: JIRA_WEBHOOK_SECRET_REF is undefined — incoming webhook signatures cannot be verified. On a closed-network Data Center installation this is normal: tickets work through the sweep and polling.
config.detail.webhook.configured: JIRA_WEBHOOK_SECRET_REF is defined — incoming webhook signatures can be verified. (The secret's value never reaches the panel.)

config.fix.clarify.no_bot_account: TEST the Jira connection under Settings > Connections (the identity is learned automatically), or fill in MAESTRO_BOT_ACCOUNT_ID by hand.
config.fix.clarify.no_ticket_reader: Ticket reading exists on the Jira Cloud and Jira Data Center drivers; check the Jira connection on the Settings screen.
config.fix.gate_channel.comment_only: If you want operators to be able to decide by dragging the card on the board too, fill in the "Let a gate decision be given by status too" section on the Listening rules screen.
config.fix.gate_channel.conflict: On the Listening rules screen pick a gate status Maestro will never move the ticket to on its own — one that appears in none of the five mapping rows above it.
config.fix.intake.no_reader: Comment reading is offered by the Jira Cloud and Jira Data Center drivers. If the installed driver is neither, approvals must be given from the panel.
config.fix.intake.webhook_only: Turn on "we ask Jira" in the setup wizard; that setting is saved from the panel and needs no restart.
config.fix.jira_driver.none: Fill in EXACTLY ONE in .env and restart the services: Data Center → JIRA_BASE_URL, Cloud → JIRA_CLOUD_BASE_URL (+ MAESTRO_BOT_EMAIL).
config.fix.jira_driver.url_is_cloud: If you use Cloud, move the address to JIRA_CLOUD_BASE_URL (+ MAESTRO_BOT_EMAIL), DELETE the JIRA_BASE_URL line and restart the services.
config.fix.jira_driver.url_not_cloud: If you use Data Center, move the address to JIRA_BASE_URL, DELETE the JIRA_CLOUD_BASE_URL line and restart the services. If you front Cloud with your own proxy, this row can be ignored.
config.fix.pool_exit.missing: On the Listening rules screen open the rule, keep the "Jira statuses" switch on and put NON-pool statuses into "When information is missing" and "When analysis goes to approval" (or "When work is done" without gates). Saving is now refused while these are blank.
config.fix.rule_identity.internal_key: First run the Jira connection's test on the Settings screen (it learns the correct username from Jira), then press "Align bot account" on the Listening rules screen.
config.fix.rule_identity.no_connection: Run the Jira connection's test on the Settings screen; the bot account is learned then and can be compared against the rules.
config.fix.rule_identity.stale: Run the Jira connection's test on the Settings screen, then press "Align bot account" on the Listening rules screen — the rules' bot account is set to the connection's.
config.fix.status_map.comment_only: If you want tickets to move on the board, add a "Jira status" map to a rule on the Listening rules screen.
config.fix.status_map.unsupported: Status moving is offered by the Jira Cloud and Jira Data Center drivers. Check the Jira connection on the Settings screen, or remove the maps from the rules.
config.fix.sweep.off_driver: Check the Jira connection on the Settings & connections screen; the work driver is decided by the Jira address in .env.
config.fix.sweep.off_setting: To turn it on, delete the JIRA_DISCOVER_MS line from .env or set JIRA_DISCOVER_MS=300000 (5 min) and restart the services.
config.fix.variant_models.cloud: Run ./ajan-modelleri.sh on the server to see the report, and ./ajan-modelleri.sh --onar to repair; or pick your organisation's own model for each variant on the Agents screen.
config.fix.webhook.absent: If you will use webhooks, fill in JIRA_WEBHOOK_SECRET_REF in .env and write the secret to the secret store. If not, having the sweep and polling on is enough.
config.tani.partial: This report does NOT include SERVICE LOGS. The panel runs inside a container and cannot reach the logs of the other services (postgres, temporal, worker, nginx) — a deliberate security decision. To see the logs too, run ./tani.sh on the server. You CANNOT conclude "the logs are fine" from this report.

detail.restart.body: Its record and steps are here, but the engine has no execution for it: retention may have expired or the run may have died. No approval or rejection can be given in this state. Restarting keeps the old run's journal and takes the ticket through intake again.
detail.restart.confirm_body: The old run is retired — its journal, steps and evidence package are preserved exactly as they are, it only leaves the board's default view. The ticket starts again under the listening rule's current settings.

detail.restart.release_hint: The run is stopped and retired, NO new run is opened; if the ticket still sits in the pool status assigned to the bot, the next sweep round takes it again.
detail.restart.stuck_body: The run failed, was handed over or is stuck. Restarting keeps the old run's journal and takes the ticket through the flow again with the listening rule's current settings; a still-running execution is stopped first.

help.feature.approval.body: There are two equivalent ways to approve a gate: leave a comment containing only /approve on the ticket, OR assign the ticket to the Maestro bot. Both go through the same authorisation and separation-of-duties checks; use whichever fits your team's habits.
help.feature.approval.title: Two ways to approve: an /approve comment or assigning to the bot
help.feature.auditcsv.body: On the Audit screen you can filter the records by From/To date, Actor, Action and free text; 'Download CSV' exports EVERYTHING the filter matches (no paging) as one file — this is the file you hand to a regulator or internal audit.
help.feature.auditcsv.title: Audit report: filter and download as CSV
help.feature.autostart.body: When you bind a Jira project, Maestro starts working on its own with ready-made listening rules: eligible tickets enter the flow without any extra setup step. To narrow the rules, use Setup → Project binding → Listening rules.
help.feature.autostart.title: Auto-start and ready-made rules
help.feature.clarify.body: When information is missing the bot never invents it: it writes its question as a comment on the ticket and hands the work back to you. Write your answer as a comment and assign the ticket back to the bot — it continues where it left off; no forms, the whole loop lives inside Jira.
help.feature.clarify.title: Clarification loop: the bot asks, you answer
help.feature.training.body: A document you upload under Agents → an agent → Knowledge trains ONLY that agent (e.g. template samples for the analysis agent alone). Documents uploaded to the Knowledge library are available to every agent — company-wide standards belong there.
help.feature.training.title: Agent training: per-agent or shared knowledge
help.jira.approve.body: To approve a run waiting at a gate, leave a comment containing only /approve. No other text may be in the comment. To reject, write /reject <reason> — the agent corrects course in the same session rather than starting over.
help.jira.approve.title: 4. How to approve

help.jira.no_rules: No listening rule is defined yet. Until one exists, no ticket reaches Maestro — bind a project from the Project binding screen so the ready-made rules are installed.
help.jira.open.body: For a ticket to reach Maestro, ALL three conditions below must hold: it must be opened in the right project, be of the right type, and be assigned to the bot account shown below.
help.jira.open.note: If all three do not hold, the ticket never reaches Maestro. Put the account id below in the assignee field; Jira resolves it to the bot user.
help.jira.open.title: 1. How to open a ticket
help.jira.perms.title: 3. Service-account permissions
help.jira.sub: read from the live listening rules — if a rule changes, this text changes with it
help.jira.title: What do I need to do in Jira?
help.jira.webhook.body: Ask your Jira admin for one global webhook, once: Jira Settings → System → Webhooks → Create a WebHook. No per-project webhook and no JQL upkeep are needed; the filtering lives inside Maestro.
help.jira.webhook.secret: The value you put in the webhook's secret field is held on the Maestro side in the Vault entry named by JIRA_WEBHOOK_SECRET_REF (default: kv/jira#webhook). Do not type the secret into Studio — write it to Vault.
help.jira.webhook.title: 2. How to register the webhook
help.jira.webhook.url_note: Replace <maestro-server> with the address Jira can reach Maestro on (the backend's address, not Studio's).
help.page.aiusage.example: You see this month's dollar spend, notice one account's quota is 'exhausted', and add capacity.
help.page.aiusage.fields:
**Cost / Traffic** (tabs).
**Cost tab** — counters: API spend ($) · Quota-covered calls · Tokens. Below, a 'Gateway call log' table (Time · Run · Role · Driver · In/Out tokens · Cost · Data class).
**Traffic tab** — Subscription pool table (Account · Driver · State: ready/cooling/exhausted/disabled · Windows %) and Recent calls table.
Subscription calls draw from quota (shown 'from quota'), API calls from dollars; deliberately separate.
help.page.aiusage.how: Two tabs: 'Cost' (dollar spend) and 'Traffic' (call volume/quota). Subscription calls draw from quota, API calls from dollars; the two are deliberately shown separately.
help.page.aiusage.purpose: How much AI usage costs and the state of the quota — budget tracking.
help.page.aiusage.title: AI usage & cost
help.page.audit.example: An auditor opens an approval event and confirms the record is consistent in the chain and who approved it.
help.page.audit.fields:
**Verify chain now** (button) — re-hashes the record to check consistency; shows how many records were checked.
**Chain status badge** — Consistent / Broken / Not verified. An 'ok' that verified nothing drops to amber, not green.
**Audit records** (table) — # · Time · Actor · Action (badge: approve/reject/kill-switch…) · Subject · Hash.
This screen is read-only (auditor role); nothing is written, even 'verify' only recomputes.
help.page.audit.how: It lists events; it also verifies the chain is unbroken by re-hashing it. It never says 'ok' without verifying anything — verification shows exactly how many records it checked.
help.page.audit.purpose: Who did what and when — a tamper-evident (hash-chained) record. For compliance and audit.
help.page.audit.title: Audit trail
help.page.dash.example: You come in the morning, see the '3 jobs await your approval' counter, and click one from the list to open its detail.
help.page.dash.fields:
**Counters (top)** — Active workflow · Waiting at a gate · Completed · Total. Not clickable, status only.
**Needs attention** — the 5 most urgent jobs (failures first, then longest-waiting approvals). Click a row → that job's detail.
**All workflows** — full filterable list.
**While setup is incomplete:** a '5 steps to get running' guide appears (connections → bind a project → Jira webhook → train the agent → watch); each step reads its own state and turns ✓ when done. You can close it with 'Got it, hide this' — if the setup is still incomplete, a short note stays on the Panel.
help.page.dash.how: It reads the status of every workflow and turns it into counters at the top; it surfaces what 'needs attention' (failures first, then the longest-waiting approvals). While the setup is incomplete — even when jobs already exist — it shows the 'where to start' guide.
help.page.dash.purpose: Your home screen. How many jobs are running, how many await your approval, how many finished, how many got stuck — all at a glance.
help.page.dash.title: Dashboard
help.page.doctemplate.example: You upload the bank's letterhead Word template; the screen says 'logo placeholder missing', you fix it and re-upload.
help.page.doctemplate.fields:
**Upload template (.docx)** (file, admin only) — uploads the institution's Word template; only .docx.
**Download** — download the current template. **Styles read from template** — style names read from the .docx.
**Recognised placeholders** (table) — Placeholder ({{ticket}}) · What goes in · Location · Status (found / missing).
**Section mapping** (table) — each analysis section maps to a placeholder ({{section:N}}).
**Recently produced documents** — files, date, template version.
Without a template production does not stop; it falls back to a plain cover but tells you.
help.page.doctemplate.how: You upload a .docx; the screen recognises the placeholders inside it (like {{section:1}}) and warns about missing ones. Without a template production does not stop — it falls back to a plain cover, but tells you.
help.page.doctemplate.purpose: Lets the analysis be embedded into your institution's own Word template (cover, logo, letterhead, approval table). Maestro only fills the placeholders.
help.page.doctemplate.title: Document template (Word)
help.page.eval.example: (Target) A new analysis prompt is tested on 50 old tickets; if the score drops on 3, the manager decides with a written reason.
help.page.eval.fields:
**Reference ticket pool** (table) — ID · Source ticket · Type · Expected behaviour · Last score. The past tickets the test runs against.
**Last eval run** (table) — ID · Current version score · New version score · Result (regressed / no regression).
**Release decision** (admin) — if there is a regression, **Reason** (required) + **Ship** / **Block**. Shipping without a reason is refused server-side.
NOTE: the backend that runs the test is not wired here, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.eval.how: It runs against the reference ticket set and shows the score; if it drops, a manager says 'ship anyway with a reason' or 'block'. NOTE: the backend that runs the test is not wired in this environment, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.eval.purpose: Testing an agent/prompt change before publishing it, against a reference set of past real tickets — to catch a drop in quality.
help.page.eval.title: Release quality test
help.page.evidence.example: An auditor enters 'ODEME-142' and checks the hash of the PDF that job produced and its approval chain.
help.page.evidence.fields:
**Ticket** (text) — the ticket key whose evidence package you want (e.g. UGURPAY-142).
Entering it opens three cards:
**Package contents** (table) — File · Type · sha256 · Size. Every produced file is sealed with a hash.
**Audit summary** — Ticket · Run · Created · Template version · File count · Retention · Object Lock.
**Approval chain** (table) — Gate · Decision · Decided by · Separation of duties · Time.
There is deliberately no download button; Studio invents no 'compliant ✓' claim.
help.page.evidence.how: You enter a ticket key; the list of documents that job produced and the signature of each approval step come up. It does not invent a 'compliant ✓' summary; it shows the real status of each decision.
help.page.evidence.purpose: The audit file of a finished job: the files produced (hash + size) and the signed approval chain. Proof that a job was done by the rules.
help.page.evidence.title: Evidence package
help.page.health.example: You see the 'Engine: degraded' line and notify the relevant team.
help.page.health.fields:
**Overall status badge** — All healthy / Some degraded / A service is down (decided by the server).
**Services** (table) — Service (BFF · Pilot · PostgreSQL · Temporal · Jira · Runner service · Worker · Storage…) · Status (healthy/degraded/down) · Version · Last checked · Note.
Refreshes every 60 seconds. Monitoring only, nothing to fill in.
help.page.health.how: It probes the services regularly; the overall status (healthy / degraded / down) is decided by the server. If there is a problem, it shows which service is affected.
help.page.health.purpose: Whether the services Maestro depends on (database, Jira, engine) are up.
help.page.health.title: System health
help.page.knowledge.example: You upload the note 'Statement filters must always be limited to the last 12 months'; the AI takes it into account in the next analysis.
help.page.knowledge.fields:
**Learning sources (top):**
**Title** — short name (e.g. 'Statement screen rules').
**Content** — the rule/knowledge text; inserted verbatim into the analysis prompt.
**Add** — saves and pushes to the running pilot; taken into account in new analyses.
**Status column (✓ learning / off)** — click to include/exclude from analysis; the note is not deleted.
**Delete** — removes the note.
**Search (bottom):**
**Search** — search shared knowledge files. Results: File · Source · Data class · App · Updated by. Confidential records you cannot see are noted as '{n} withheld'.
help.page.knowledge.how: You add a learning note (title + content); notes marked 'learning' are put in front of the AI as 'things to watch for' when a new analysis is prepared. Turning it off does not delete the note, it just excludes it from the analysis.
help.page.knowledge.purpose: Two jobs: (1) search shared knowledge files, (2) 'learning sources' — upload notes the AI takes into account in a new analysis.
help.page.knowledge.title: Knowledge library
help.page.notify.example: For an approval unanswered for 3 days, the system reminds the owner first, then the backup via Teams; still no answer, it reports to you.
help.page.notify.fields:
**1 · Event → channel** (table) — which event (gate opened, CI red, escalation, kill-switch…) goes to which channel (Jira/Teams). Edit with 'Edit mapping'.
**2 · Pending approvals** (table) — Ticket · Gate · Wait time (7+ days red, 3+ amber) · Last action.
**3 · Reminder ladder** — 'Edit ladder': each step has an **Hour** threshold + a **channel**, chained with arrows.
**4 · Delegation chain** (table) — Role · Primary · Backup · Last resort.
**Teams webhook URL** (admin only) — the channel's Incoming Webhook; shown masked. Saving empty deletes it.
No step auto-rejects a job — the last step is a report to a manager.
help.page.notify.how: You edit the event → channel routing, the reminder ladder (hours/days) and the delegation chain. No step auto-rejects a job — the last step is a report to a manager; the gate never closes on its own.
help.page.notify.purpose: Makes sure an approval is not forgotten: who is reminded, through which channel (Jira/Teams), and who it is handed to if there is no answer.
help.page.notify.title: Notifications & escalation
help.page.params.example: You propose changing 'second approval on high-risk jobs'; the old value applies until a second manager confirms it.
help.page.params.fields:
**Table** — Parameter (name + '4-eyes' badge + description) · Value · Scope · Version · Changed by · Inspect/Edit.
If a proposal is pending, 'awaiting approval' + who proposed it is shown under the value (the old value stays live).
**Editing:** **New value** (text/number/boolean/list/JSON by type).
**Guarded (4-eyes) parameters:** saving files a proposal; the old value stays live until a second manager confirms the identical value. You cannot approve your own proposal.
Examples: approval gate set, security block level, merge mode, escalation ladder, Teams webhook (masked).
help.page.params.how: When you change a setting, the 'guarded' (four-eyes) ones file a proposal, and the old value stays live until a second manager confirms the identical value. Who proposed it and the current value are shown clearly.
help.page.params.purpose: Operational settings like gate sets, approval thresholds, reminder ladders — all in one place.
help.page.params.title: Parameters
help.page.pii.example: An auditor sees 'the ID field was masked in 1,240 calls recently, no exempt agent' and confirms compliance.
help.page.pii.fields:
**Today** (counters) — Masked calls (masked/total, %) · Masked fields · On-prem calls (unmasked because they don't leave the network) · Exempt variants.
**Archive badge** — 'archive written masked' (green) / 'archive unmasked — audit finding' (red).
**Masking rules** (table) — Type (field/pattern) · Matcher (e.g. 'tckn' — NOT the value) · Strategy (hash/partial/redact) · Hit count.
Masking is done on the server; this screen shows no real/plaintext value, only numbers and rules.
help.page.pii.how: It reports how many fields were masked in how many calls, and how many times each rule fired. Masking is done on the server; this screen neither asks for nor shows any sample/plaintext value.
help.page.pii.purpose: Proves that personal data (national ID, IBAN, etc.) is masked on the way to the AI — as numbers and rules only, never showing the data itself.
help.page.pii.title: PII masking
help.page.projects.example: You add the new 'ODEME' project, another manager approves it, then you add the rule 'only take Bug-type tickets'.
help.page.projects.fields:
**Tab 1 · Add application** — a single form, all dropdowns:
**Jira connection** — one of your Jira connections.
**Jira project** — that connection's projects (e.g. 'PAY · Payments').
**SCM connection** — GitHub/Azure; **Repo** — that connection's repos.
**Platform profile** — Node.js/web · .NET/Windows · iOS/macOS · Android.
**Trigger mode** — Opt-in (recommended) / Automatic. **Gate set** — Risk-tiered (recommended) / Always 6. **Merge mode** — Human-merge (recommended) / Auto.
**Run dry run** (button, required) — shows where recent tickets would land; you cannot submit without it.
**Send for admin approval** — sends the package to a second manager (does not go live).
**Tab 2 · Bound projects & approval** — pending-approvals table (Approve/Reject) and bound-projects table with a 'Status' column ('⚠ needs a listening rule').
**Tab 3 · Listening rules** — described separately below.
help.page.projects.how: Three tabs: ①Add application (pick a Jira project + code repo) → ②Approve (a second manager approves, the project is bound) → ③Listening rule (which tickets to process). If something is already bound, the page opens on the list.
help.page.projects.purpose: Binding a Jira project to Maestro — i.e. telling it 'handle this project's tickets'. Gathers the 3 steps on one page.
help.page.projects.title: Project binding
help.page.runners.example: (Target) You see 'Linux pool 4/16 full, 2 machines unreachable' and spot the capacity problem.
help.page.runners.fields:
**Pool counters** — per pool: usage (busy/capacity) and how many machines are unreachable.
**Machines** (table) — Machine (runner id + pool) · Pool (linux/windows…) · Slots (active/capacity) · Status (idle/busy/draining/unreachable).
Unreachable machines are moved to the top and flagged red.
NOTE: the backend that reports machine status is not wired here, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.runners.how: It reads the machines and pool usage regularly and highlights 'how many machines are unreachable'. NOTE: the backend that reports machine status is not wired in this environment, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.runners.purpose: The fleet of machines where agents run code in isolation; unreachable machines are moved to the top and flagged.
help.page.runners.title: Worker machines
help.page.sandbox.example: (Target) You see the session 'ODEME-142 · held by a human · 320MB' and understand a person is still in that workspace.
help.page.sandbox.fields:
**Open sessions** (table) — Ticket · Runner · Session state (active / resumable / held by a human) · Size · Last access.
For security the session CONTENTS (raw ticket text could leak) are not shown, and there is no manual DELETE — cleanup runs on its own schedule; 'held by a human' is kept separate.
NOTE: the backend that reports session status is not wired here, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.sandbox.how: It lists open sessions. For security it does not show session contents (raw ticket text could leak) and offers no manual delete — cleanup runs on its own schedule. NOTE: the backend that reports session status is not wired in this environment, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.sandbox.purpose: The isolated workspaces agents are working in right now and their states (active / resumable / held by a human).
help.page.sandbox.title: Live sessions
help.page.security.example: (Target) A scan finds an API key in a PR; the finding is listed as 'critical' at the top and the job is held at a gate.
help.page.security.fields:
**Findings** (table, most severe first) — Severity (critical/high/medium/low) · Ticket · Tool (Semgrep/Trivy/Gitleaks) · Finding · File:line · Status (passed/failed/scanner didn't run) · Date.
**Finding text** is hidden by default — 'Show scanner text' reveals it (raw output may contain secrets).
If the scanner couldn't run it is not counted 'clean', it shows red (fail-closed).
NOTE: the backend that writes scan results is not wired here, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.security.how: It lists findings from the flow's scan step; if the scanner could not run at all, it does not count that as 'clean' — it shows red. NOTE: the backend that writes scan results is not wired in this environment, so the page appears empty for now.
help.page.security.purpose: Shows security findings in AI-written code (leaked key, vulnerable library, etc.), most severe first.
help.page.security.title: Security scans
help.page.settings.example: You enter the Jira connection and validate it with 'Test'; the test also auto-captures the bot's identity (accountId), used later in a listening rule.
help.page.settings.fields:
**Connections (top):** **➕ Add connection** (admin). Table — Connection · Status (connected/error/untested) · Address · Token (last 4) · 🔌 Test / Edit / Delete.
**Add form:** **Id** (lowercase-dash, e.g. jira) · **Type** (Jira Cloud/Jira DC/GitHub/Azure DevOps/OpenRouter/Anthropic/Vault/SMTP/Storage) · **Display name** · **Address (URL)** · **Auth** (Basic email:token / Bearer / PAT / API key) · **Enabled** · **Token** (write-only, then masked).
**🔌 Test** — validates live with the stored credential; a Jira test also auto-captures the bot's accountId (used in a listening rule).
**Emergency stop (bottom, admin only):** ① Stop new intake · ② Stop everything · Return to normal. Each requires a **reason** + confirmation; written to the audit trail.
help.page.settings.how: When adding a connection you enter URL + token and validate it live with 'Test'; the token is stored encrypted, only its last 4 digits shown. The kill switch has two levels (stop new work / stop everything).
help.page.settings.purpose: Maestro's connections to external systems (Jira, GitHub, Azure, AI provider) and the 'kill switch' that stops everything in an emergency.
help.page.settings.title: Settings & connections
help.page.template.example: You add a required section called 'Risk Assessment'; every analysis from then on also fills it in.
help.page.template.fields:
**+ Add section** — adds a new section (e.g. Scope, Risk).
**Section title** — the visible name; the schema key is derived automatically.
**Expected format** — free text / bullet list / table / impact matrix.
**Description (for humans)** — shown under the heading.
**Instruction to AI** — tells the agent how to fill this section; goes verbatim into the prompt.
**Required** (checkbox) — if set and missing, the analysis doesn't reach approval, the agent regenerates (fail-closed).
**Example text (few-shot)** — a 'good answer' example for the agent.
**↑ ↓ ✕** — move / remove. **Preview** — preview the document.
**Save as new version** — publishes the change as a new version; running jobs finish on the old one.
help.page.template.how: You add, remove and reorder sections; each section gets an instruction telling the AI what to write and an example. Saving publishes a new version; running jobs finish on the version they started with, unbroken.
help.page.template.purpose: You decide which sections the AI's analysis report will have (e.g. Purpose, Impact, Risk, Things to test).
help.page.template.title: Analysis template
help.page.users.example: You add a developer to the 'tech-lead' group; the screen shows they can now make gate decisions.
help.page.users.fields:
**➕ Add user** (admin). **Table** — User · Directory group · Maestro role (coloured badge) · Account (active/disabled) · Edit/Disable.
**Add/edit form:** **Username** (e.g. ayse.kaya) · **Display name** · **Password** (min 8 chars, upper/lower+digit+symbol; weak ones list the violations).
**Team / role** (checkbox list) — you assign the person to teams, the PERMISSION COMES FROM THE TEAM (roles not set by hand): Platform admins→admin · Tech leads→tech-lead · Product owners→product-owner · QA→qa · Developers→developer · Auditors→viewer. A live 'roles to grant' preview is shown.
**Disable** — closes the account (does not delete; keeps the name for audit); blocks login, ends sessions.
Separation-of-duties (SoD) rules are also listed here.
help.page.users.how: You add/edit users (weak passwords are refused); the role comes automatically from the assigned group (roles are not set by hand). An unknown group is shown neutral, so it never implies the wrong permission colour.
help.page.users.purpose: Who has which permission. You assign users to groups; the role comes from the group. 'Separation of duties' (the same person cannot both do and approve) is enforced here.
help.page.users.title: Users & roles
help.page.variants.example: You add the instruction 'do not make things up where unsure, ask explicitly' to the analysis agent and publish a new version.
help.page.variants.fields:
**Add agent definition** (button, admin) — a new agent definition; publishes version 1 on save.
**Table** — Agent definition · Role · Platform · Model · Active version · Knowledge source · Quality score. Click a row → detail.
**Add form:** **Variant id** (lowercase-dash, e.g. analyst-web) · **Role** (of 7) · **Platform** · **Model** · **Persona text** · **Knowledge files** · **Version note**.
**Detail:** Persona / Knowledge / Versions tabs. **Publish new version** — change model/persona/knowledge into a new version; a published version is never edited in place.
help.page.variants.how: You set an agent's persona and model and publish it. Versions are immutable; a new version is published, rolled back in one step, and running jobs finish on the version they started with.
help.page.variants.purpose: Each AI agent's 'personality' (how it behaves) and which model it uses. You manage the analysis and engineering agents here.
help.page.variants.title: Agent definitions
help.setup_step.permissions: Service account permissions: Browse, Comment, Edit (label), Assign, Create/Link Issue. No workflow change, custom field or plugin is required — no Jira admin burden on the institution.
help.subtitle: Each menu category is a tab; every page is explained as 'what it's for / how it works / example'.
help.summary: You write a ticket in Jira; Maestro reads it, asks in a comment if something is missing, and writes the analysis. You approve it; it writes the code in an isolated sandbox and really runs the tests, then opens a PR. A human approves the PR and it is merged. Nothing is released to production — release stays the institution's own process.
help.tabs.label: Help categories
help.title: Help — how to use
intake.accepted: Maestro has picked up {ticket}. The analysis is being prepared; progress is posted here as comments, and any approval will be asked for on this ticket.
intake.manual_completion: I could not assess this request automatically (the model response was unusable). Please complete the missing details by hand.
intake.not_opted_in: {ticket} was not started: this project only accepts labelled tickets. Add the "{label}" label to the ticket and try again.
issues.col.question: Question
issues.filter_hint: The filter applies to the records on this page only.
jira.analysis_delivered: The analysis for {ticket} is complete and approved ({risk} risk). The ticket has been handed back to the requester; writing code is outside this flow.
jira.analysis_docs_failed: The analysis for {ticket} was delivered, but the Word/PDF document could not be attached to the ticket. The full analysis is in the comment on this ticket; contact the Maestro team for a document copy.
jira.clarification:
One thing needs clarifying before I can continue:

{question}
jira.closed: {ticket} is complete. The documents produced and the decision history are in the audit trail.
jira.gate_group_none: no approval group configured — any authorised person with ticket access decides
jira.gate_open: Maestro is waiting for approval at gate {gate}. Deciding group: {group}. To approve, comment /approve on this ticket; to reject, comment /reject <reason>. IMPORTANT: the decision must be given as a comment — moving the ticket to another status does not open the gate and the run keeps waiting.
jira.gate_open_with_status: Maestro is waiting for approval at gate {gate}. Deciding group: {group}. EITHER WAY WORKS, whichever comes first. (1) BY COMMENT: comment /approve to approve, /reject <reason> to reject. (2) BY STATUS: moving the ticket to '{approve}' counts as an approval; moving it to '{returnTo}' sends the analysis back to be rewritten (this is not a rejection — the context is kept). Approval by status only works where Jira can tell us who moved it; if it does not take effect, comment /approve on the ticket.
jira.gate_unaddressed: WARNING: Maestro opened gate {gate} to the group {group}, but that group has no registered users — the reminder could not be sent to anyone. The run is still waiting and will not advance on its own. Add at least one user to {group} in the admin panel, then close the gate by commenting /approve or /reject <reason> on this ticket.
jira.handover: ⚠ Maestro handed this ticket over to a human: {reason}. The run journal is in Studio; once fixed, restart it from Studio or return the ticket to the pool status.
jira.status_move_failed: ⚠ Maestro could not move this ticket to '{status}': {reason}. The ticket stayed in the robot's pool — please move it to '{status}' by hand, or fix the transition/permission in Jira.
journal.actor.ai.label: AI
journal.actor.human.label: Human
journal.actor.system.label: System
journal.append_only: Append-only: entries are never modified. This is the raw material of the evidence package.
journal.empty_hint: Every step is appended here as the flow proceeds.
killswitch.card.sub: Safely halts Maestro when something goes wrong. Admin only · reason required · written to the audit log. Operated from here only.
killswitch.card.title: Emergency stop (kill switch)
killswitch.confirm.all: A stop signal will go to every running ticket; open approval gates keep waiting. The persistent analysis sandbox stays up. This cannot be undone: reopening does not resurrect stopped work.
killswitch.confirm.audit_warning: This is written permanently to the audit log with your reason and affects the whole platform.
killswitch.confirm.intake_only: New work will pause. Running work finishes uninterrupted; the analysis sandbox stays up.
killswitch.confirm.off: Maestro will start taking work again.
killswitch.confirm.title: Confirm emergency stop
killswitch.indicator.open: Emergency stop — operated from the System health screen
killswitch.note.admin_only: The emergency stop is available to the admin role only.
killswitch.note.delegated: This session is held by an AI tool on your behalf; the emergency stop is a human-only channel. The MCP surface can only raise a proposal.
listening.agent.hint: Which agent variant runs this flow. Leave as "Default agent" to let the platform pick.
listening.confirm.delete_desc: The rule {project} · {trigger} will be deleted. Tickets matching it are no longer picked up; runs already started are not affected.
listening.detail.label: Rule detail
listening.empty: No rules yet — add one above.
listening.flow.hint.analiz: Produces the analysis document only; no code, no PR. For requests that need investigation.
listening.flow.hint.duzeltme: Small bug fix: skips the analysis-approval gate and goes straight to coding. The PR is still reviewed.
listening.flow.hint.gelistirme: Full pipeline: analysis → approval → code → PR → merge. For new features / enhancements.
listening.form.allowed_statuses_empty_wa: WARNING: no status picked — this rule has NO status gate. Every ticket assigned to the bot is processed wherever it sits on the board (closed, archived, not yet written). Picking at least one status is strongly recommended.
listening.form.allowed_statuses_hint: A ticket is processed ONLY while it sits in one of the statuses you picked. Even one assigned to the bot is left alone in any other status.
listening.form.allowed_statuses_manual: Separate status names with commas and spell them EXACTLY as the Jira board does (case included).
listening.form.allowed_statuses_pick_pro: Pick a PROJECT above first — status names are read live from that project's Jira board.
listening.form.allowed_statuses_unavaila: The status list could NOT be read from Jira (no connection, or Jira did not answer). You can type them by hand below, but testing the Jira connection under Settings & connections first is recommended — a hand-typed status that does not match the board's spelling exactly will match no ticket.
listening.form.assignee_hint: The Jira identity (accountId) of the Maestro Bot account tickets are assigned to. Copy it from the bot's Jira profile URL or from the connection settings.
listening.form.assignee_hint_auto: Filled in automatically from the connection (Maestro Bot). You don't need to change it; edit it by hand only if you use a different bot.
listening.form.editing_which: Editing: {project} · {trigger}. The fields below show this rule as it stands TODAY; use "Test" to try it and "Save" to write over it.
listening.form.incomplete: Project, bot user and value cannot be empty.
listening.form.jira_connection_hint: Value and status lists are read through this connection. It is not stored on the rule — the rule is identified by its bot account; the connection that knows that account is suggested.
listening.form.matchValue_hint: Type it exactly as the issue type or status name reads in Jira (e.g. "Bug"). If it differs, the rule matches no ticket.
listening.form.matchValue_hint_auto: Real values pulled from Jira — pick from the list. No risk of a typo.
listening.form.priority_hint: When several rules match one ticket the lower number wins. Empty = 100.
listening.form.priority_invalid: Priority must be a whole number between 0 and 10000.
listening.form.project_hint: Only bound projects are listed. A rule cannot be added to a project that is not bound.
listening.form.project_none_hint: No bound projects yet. Bind one from the "Add application" tab first.
listening.form.sub: Decide which tickets get processed: project, bot user, match condition and what to do.
listening.form.title: Add a rule
listening.gate_status.approval_note: Note: approval BY STATUS only works where Jira can tell us who moved the ticket (a registered webhook, or a poller that can read the changelog). Where the identity cannot be read, approval is not carried — comment /approve there instead. "Send back to analysis" always works: it lets nobody approve anything.
listening.gate_status.comment_only: Status mapping is off: the gate closes only through "/approve" and "/reject" comments. To approve by moving the ticket, turn on the switch above and fill in "When the work is done".
listening.gate_status.derived_approve: Approval — moving the ticket to {status} counts the same as writing "/approve". {from}
listening.gate_status.derived_return: Send back to analysis — moving the ticket to {status} has the analysis rewritten. {from}
listening.gate_status.empty_warning: Both edges of the gate are EMPTY. Because the "when work is done" and "on rejection"/"when work starts" fields above are unset, moving the ticket to a status in Jira will not open the gate or send the analysis back; decisions come only from /approve and /reject comments on the ticket. Fill in the status map above if you want to drive this from the board.
listening.gate_status.from.gateApproveSt: (from the approval status set separately on this rule)
listening.gate_status.from.gateReturnSta: (from the send-back status set separately on this rule)
listening.gate_status.from.onReview: (from the "when analysis goes to review" field)
listening.gate_status.intro: The five rows above say where Maestro MOVES the ticket. The same rows read in reverse too: when YOU move the ticket there, Maestro takes it as a decision. Nothing extra to fill in — the two edges of the gate are derived from those five fields and shown below. They apply while an analysis approval gate is open, and the /approve comment path stays exactly as it was; whichever arrives first closes the gate.
listening.gate_status.no_gate_flow: The bug-fix flow has no analysis-approval gate; moving the ticket is not read as a decision on this rule.
listening.gate_status.review_clash: A gate edge is the same as the "when analysis goes to review" status: {values}. The gate OPENS in that status, so moving the ticket there is not a decision — it is the ticket waiting at the gate. That edge does not take effect; pick a different status.
listening.gate_status.review_missing: "When analysis goes to approval" is BLANK: when the analysis finishes the ticket is not moved to any status and the board never shows work awaiting approval — it reads as "the robot did not move it". Put your approval-queue status (e.g. analysisapproval) in that field.
listening.gate_status.title: Gate decision: approving by moving the ticket
listening.gates.default: No selection — by risk tier (today's behaviour)
listening.gates.engineering_only: This gate opens only on code-writing flows (fix/feature); this rule runs the analysis flow, so it will not open even if selected.
listening.gates.explain: Which approvals Maestro should WAIT for on runs started by this rule. With no selection today's behaviour continues: gates open according to the risk tier the analysis finds. Select none and Maestro waits for no approval — the right choice when approvals are given by moving the ticket's status in Jira.
listening.gates.none_selected: No approval gate selected — this rule proceeds without waiting for approval.
listening.gates.ownerless: Open gates without an owner (do not ask for an approval group)
listening.gates.ownerless_explain: When on, Maestro does not open the gate in the name of an approval group and does not check group membership. The decider's identity is still written to the audit trail, and the rule that one person cannot sign both analysis gates still applies. Turn this on when Jira's own permission scheme carries the approval authority.
listening.gates.title: Approval gates
listening.repomap.title: Repository map (which ticket goes to which repo)
listening.repomap.summary_incomplete: ON but no rows — will not be saved
listening.repomap.explain: A Jira project binds to one application. When the same project spans several repositories, a field on the ticket says which one (e.g. Business Family). Pick the field and map each value to an application. An unmapped value goes to the project binding's application.
listening.repomap.enable: Choose the repository by a ticket field
listening.repomap.field_hint: Read from the connection; custom fields first.
listening.repomap.field_manual_hint: The field list could not be read; type the field id (visible in Jira's field settings, e.g. customfield_10234).
listening.repomap.branch_hint: The environment branch the code lands on; empty = the application's default.
listening.repomap.incomplete: The map is on but has no complete row (value + application). Fill a row or turn the map off.
listening.identity.internal: {count} rules carry a bot account shaped like `jirauser12345`. That is Jira Data Center's INTERNAL handle — Jira searches resolve an assignee by USERNAME (`ugyildiz`). A search made with the internal handle finds no tickets, and Jira answers with an empty result rather than an error, so the sweep silently brings back nothing. First run the Jira connection's test on the Settings screen, then press the button below.
listening.identity.stale: {count} rules carry an identity OTHER than the bot account the Jira connection knows ({account}). The sweep writes the rule's identity straight into the Jira search: an identity that matches nobody makes Jira return an empty result, not an error — so these rules silently bring back no tickets.
listening.intro: When a ticket matches a rule here (in the project, assigned to the Maestro Bot, and its status/issue type matches) Maestro picks it up and runs it as the given flow type (analysis / fix / feature). With no rule, the default behaviour stands.
listening.match.assigned: Every ticket assigned to the bot
listening.match.hint.assigned: Fires when the ticket is ASSIGNED to the bot. The status restriction below still applies — being assigned is not enough on its own.
listening.match.hint.issuetype: Fires when a ticket of that TYPE is opened (e.g. "Bug", "Task").
listening.match.hint.label: Fires when that label is ADDED to the ticket. The project setting's "trigger label" used to do this; triggering is now defined only here, per rule.
listening.match.hint.status: Fires when the ticket is MOVED to that status on the board.
listening.match.label: Label
listening.probe.compare: Nothing matched the rule, but the project has open tickets. The first {count} — are the type/status/assignee/labels in your rule EXACTLY these?
listening.probe.failed: The rule could not be tested:
listening.probe.jql_label: The query the rule sends to Jira (JQL) — you can run the same one in Jira's own search box:
listening.probe.no_match: This rule currently matches no ticket.
listening.probe.no_match_hint: You can still save it — there may be no matching ticket today and one tomorrow.
listening.probe.project_empty: No open ticket was found in the project either. The project key may be wrong, or every ticket is closed.
listening.probe.reason.bindings_unreadab: the list of bound projects could not be read, so no query was sent at all.
listening.probe.reason.no_bot_account: the rule has no bot account. A search without one would cover EVERYONE's tickets in the project, so none was sent — put the Maestro bot account in the form.
listening.probe.reason.no_label: the label is empty. A label rule needs a label name before it can be searched.
listening.probe.reason.probe_not_availab: this deployment's Jira driver offers no JQL search.
listening.probe.reason.search_failed: Jira rejected the query. The usual cause is that the service account has no read permission on that project.
listening.probe.reason.unbound_project: this project is not bound to Maestro (or is paused). Not even a test query is sent to an unbound project.
listening.probe.reason.unknown: the server reported an unnamed reason.
listening.probe.stale: The form's values differ from the ones you tested — the result below now belongs to a different rule.
listening.probe.unavailable: This deployment's Jira driver offers no JQL search; the rule cannot be tested.
listening.realign.done: The bot account on {count} rules was updated to {account}.
listening.realign.none: Every rule already carries the bot account the connection knows — nothing changed.
listening.seed.desc: Set up automatically from the project's Jira issue types: bug types → Fix, the rest → Analysis. Your existing rules are never overwritten.
listening.seed.issue_types_unavailable: Jira's issue types could not be read; no rules were added. Test the connection and try again.
listening.seed.no_project: Pick a project first — the ready-made rules are installed for the project you choose.
listening.seedskip.bot_account_unknown: the bot account is unknown — the Jira connection's test has never been run
listening.seedskip.connections_unwired: no connection store is wired on this deployment
listening.seedskip.issue_types_unavailab: Jira's issue-type list could not be read
listening.seedskip.listening_unwired: no listening store is wired on this deployment
listening.seedskip.no_jira_connection: no enabled Jira connection is configured
listening.seedskip.seed_error: seeding was cut short by an unexpected error
listening.status.dead_hint: The bug-fix flow has no analysis-approval step; this moment never occurs.
listening.status.dead_warning: This rule assigns statuses to moments that never occur in the bug-fix flow: {values}. The ticket cannot be moved at those moments; if you save the rule, these values will not be written.
listening.status.enable: Also change the ticket's Jira status for this rule
listening.status.exact: Type each value exactly as the status name reads in Jira (e.g. "In Progress"). If it differs, or that transition is not possible in Jira, the flow is not interrupted; only the ticket's status stays where it is.
listening.status.hint.onDone: The work is delivered (the PR was merged, or the analysis closed). The ticket's closing status.
listening.status.hint.onNeedInfo: The moment Maestro asks the reporter a question so it can continue. Whichever status the ticket should wait in once the ball is in their court.
listening.status.hint.onRejected: An approver rejected the analysis and the work goes back to analysis. The status the ticket falls back to.
listening.status.hint.onReview: The analysis document is ready and waiting for a human to approve it. Use this to tell approval-queue work apart on the board.
listening.status.hint.onStart: The moment Maestro picks the ticket up and starts working on it. Put your in-progress status here if the board should say "someone is on this".
listening.status.intro: By default Maestro only comments on the ticket; it never moves it. Open this section to have it move the ticket into a Jira status you choose at specific points of the flow. Every line is optional on its own — where you leave it blank the ticket stays put and the flow still runs.
listening.status.onReview: When the analysis goes for approval
listening.status.reassign: Hand the ticket back to the reporter while information is missing
listening.status.reassign_hint: On some boards "waiting on the reporter" is not a status but an assignee. Tick this and Maestro reassigns the ticket to its reporter when it asks a question, instead of leaving it on the bot. Independent of the "When information is missing" line above; you can use both together.

params.description.gate_set: Which approvals to wait for on runs whose rule selected NO approval gates — per risk tier. A per-rule selection (Listening Rules screen, 'Approval gates') OVERRIDES this value. Change it away from the shipped default and every rule that made no selection uses it. Gate ids: 4 = analysis approval (product owner), 5 = analysis approval (tech lead), 9 = test scenario approval, 11 = test result approval, 12 = PR approval.
params.description.jira_command_intake: How commands written on a ticket (/approve, /reject) reach Maestro. webhook = Jira calls us (recommended, fastest, no load on Jira). poll = Maestro asks Jira at an interval (when Jira cannot reach out). both = webhook primary, polling as a fallback (most robust, most load on Jira). The interval is set by jira.poll_seconds. Step 5 of the setup wizard writes this value.
params.description.jira_discover_seconds: How often Maestro sweeps Jira for new tickets, in SECONDS. 0 turns it off. Example: 80 → 1 min 20 s. A site with a working webhook does not need it; for everyone else this is how a ticket arrives. A smaller value picks tickets up sooner and asks Jira more often.
params.description.jira_poll_seconds: How often Maestro asks Jira to read ticket comments, in SECONDS. Used only when jira.command_intake is poll or both. 0 turns polling off. A smaller value acts on an approval sooner and asks Jira more often.

setup.done.next_approve.webhook: When a run reaches an approval gate, write “/approve” on the ticket. On this install commands arrive by Jira's call; if the approval you write is not acted on, the webhook may not be registered on the Jira side — in that case change this step to “Let us ask Jira”.

setup.gate_status.intro: The five rows above say where Maestro MOVES the ticket. The same rows read in reverse too: when YOU move the ticket there, Maestro takes it as a decision. Nothing extra to fill in — the two edges of the gate are derived from those five fields and shown below. The /approve and /reject comment paths stay exactly as they were; whichever arrives first closes the gate.

setup.intake.applies_live: This setting takes effect the moment it is saved; no service restart is needed. The change is picked up by the next round at the latest.
setup.intake.applies_restart: Note: on this install the setting only takes effect after the Maestro service is restarted. Once you have saved, ask your system administrator to restart it; until then the way commands arrive does not change.
setup.intake.applies_unknown: Whether this setting applies immediately or only after a service restart could not be read. After saving, write “/approve” on a ticket and check that the work moves on; if it does not, ask your system administrator to restart the service.
setup.intake.desc.both: The webhook is the primary path; polling stands by as a safety net and catches what the webhook misses.
setup.intake.desc.poll: Maestro asks Jira “are there new comments?” at a fixed interval. Choose this when Jira cannot reach out.
setup.intake.desc.webhook: The moment a comment is written on a ticket, Jira calls Maestro. The recommended path.
setup.intake.double_guard: The same approval is never acted on twice. Both paths feed the same command handler, and every comment it acts on is recorded once as (ticket + author + comment time); the same comment arriving a second time is skipped. A decision on a gate that is already closed is refused anyway. Two approvals written by two different people are two decisions, and are treated as such.
setup.intake.global_note: This choice applies to the whole platform, not only to this project. Change it and commands arrive this way for every project Maestro is bound to.
setup.intake.intro: To approve a piece of work you write “/approve” on the ticket, and “/reject reason” to refuse it. There are two ways Maestro can read those comments: Jira tells it, or Maestro asks Jira. Choose which one this install uses. Leave this unanswered and the approval you write may never be read, and the run waits forever.
setup.intake.load_warning: Note: polling puts load on Jira. Every interval, Maestro reads the comments on the tickets of every open run — the shorter the interval, the more often Jira is asked. Jira is shared with everyone in the bank; talk to your Jira administrator before lowering this.
setup.intake.meta.both: The most robust and the most expensive: a webhook that silently stops arriving is only noticed this way. The cost is that Jira keeps being asked every interval.
setup.intake.meta.poll: For installs behind a firewall: Jira never has to reach Maestro. An approval is acted on within at most one interval, and Jira is asked once every interval.
setup.intake.meta.webhook: The fastest: an approval is acted on within seconds and Jira carries no extra load. It requires Jira to be able to reach Maestro's address, and the webhook to be registered on the Jira side.
setup.intake.no_reader: This option is not available on this install: the configured work connection cannot read ticket comments, so asking Jira cannot work. Approvals have to be given through the webhook or from the panel. Comment reading is offered by the Jira connections; check your Jira connection on the Settings & connections screen.
